title: Three Reading Approaches: read, readline, and readlines
code:
# 1. read() - entire content as single string
with open('students.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Arun,85\nPriya,92\nRahul,35\n')

file = open('students.txt', 'r')
all_content = file.read()
print('--- read() ---')
print(all_content)
file.close()

# 2. readline() - line by line
file = open('students.txt', 'r')
print('--- readline() ---')
print('First:', file.readline().strip())
print('Second:', file.readline().strip())
file.close()

# 3. readlines() - list of lines
file = open('students.txt', 'r')
print('--- readlines() ---')
lines = file.readlines()
print('List of lines:', lines)
file.close()
explanation: Demonstrates the distinct return types of read() (string), readline() (one string), and readlines() (list of strings).

title: Preserving Records: Append Mode ('a') vs Overwrite ('w')
code:
# Initial file write
file = open('log.txt', 'w')
file.write('Event 1: System Boot\n')
file.close()

# Safe append
file = open('log.txt', 'a')
file.write('Event 2: User Login\n')
file.close()

# Verify content
file = open('log.txt', 'r')
print(file.read())
file.close()
explanation: Shows how mode 'a' appends new entries to the end of a file without destroying existing log history.

title: Processing CSV File Lines with strip() and split()
code:
records = 'Arun,85\nPriya,92\nRahul,35\nMeena,78'
with open('grades.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write(records)

file = open('grades.txt', 'r')
print('Processed Student Records:')
for line in file:
    clean_line = line.strip()
    name, mark_str = clean_line.split(',')
    mark = int(mark_str)
    status = 'Pass' if mark >= 40 else 'Fail'
    print(f'  {name:<8}: {mark:>2} ({status})')
file.close()
explanation: Iterates line-by-line using low memory, cleans whitespace with strip(), and tokenizes fields using split(',').
